sounds.name: First Polyrhythm
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s guided start, “Exploring your Subharmonicon”
sounds.blurb: Four notes from Sequencer 1, stepped by two rhythms at once: two against three.
sounds.how: The manual starts here: VCO 1 alone, Sequencer 1 moving its pitch in a chromatic scale, and one rhythm generator stepping it. A second rhythm on the same sequencer adds its own steps, so the four notes fall in a pattern that only comes round again when the two rhythms meet on a downbeat. The manual sets ±2 octaves and 12-ET; the step values and tempo here are this lesson’s.

steps.title: Tune four steps
steps.why:
Give Sequencer 1 the pitch of VCO 1, and four steps that snap to the twelve notes.
- QUANTIZE 12-ET
- SEQ OCT ±2
- SEQ 1 ASSIGN OSC 1 lit
- SEQ 1 STEP 1 0 · 0 st
- SEQ 1 STEP 2 0.63 · +3 st
- SEQ 1 STEP 3 1.46 · +7 st
- SEQ 1 STEP 4 2.08 · +10 st
- Listen for: nothing yet: the sequencer waits for a rhythm and PLAY.

steps.title: A rhythm, then PLAY
steps.why:
Rhythm 1 steps Sequencer 1 on every second clock, and each step plays the envelopes (EG is on).
- RHYTHM 1 ÷2
- RHYTHM 1 SEQ 1 lit
- PLAY lit
- VCA DECAY 5 · 220 ms
- CUTOFF 6 · 1.3 kHz
- VCF EG AMT 2 · +3.2 oct
- VCF DECAY 4 · 100 ms
- Listen for: C, E♭, G, B♭ round and round, each note a soft pluck.

steps.title: Add a second rhythm
steps.why:
Rhythm 2 steps the same sequencer on every third clock. Where the two coincide it steps once.
- RHYTHM 2 ÷3
- RHYTHM 2 SEQ 1 lit
- Listen for: the four notes now limping in a two-against-three pattern that repeats every six clocks.

sounds.name: Two Against Three
sounds.ref: In the style of West African cross-rhythm
sounds.blurb: The first polyrhythm: one tune on every second sixteenth, another on every third, meeting every six.
sounds.how: Rhythm 1 divides the clock by 2 and steps Sequencer 1; Rhythm 2 divides it by 3 and steps Sequencer 2. Each step of either fires the envelopes, so you hear the two pulses woven together, with VCO 1’s four notes moving on one and VCO 2’s on the other. They meet on the downbeat every six sixteenths, and each tune comes round at its own length, so the pairing of notes keeps changing.

sounds.name: Coin-Toss Rhythm
sounds.ref: In the style of a Buchla random-voltage rhythm
sounds.blurb: A rhythm thrown like a coin: VCO 2 at audio rate in RHYTHM 1, so each clock lands on a different divisor.
sounds.how: A RHYTHM input is read at each clock. Feed it VCO 2 at audio rate and it reads wherever VCO 2’s wave happens to be: a different divisor on every sixteenth, from ÷1 to about ÷10. Whether Rhythm 1 fires is a coin toss, a little better than even, so the melody plays a rhythm that keeps changing and almost never repeats. VCO 2’s FREQ is the coin: it sits between notes, with QUANTIZE off, so its cycles never line up with the clock; move it and the rhythm changes.

sounds.name: Three Against Four
sounds.ref: In the style of Steve Reich’s interlocking pulses
sounds.blurb: A minor arpeggio on dotted eighths against a falling line on quarters, coming round every three beats.
sounds.how: Rhythm 1 at ÷3 and Rhythm 2 at ÷4 meet every twelve sixteenths, three beats, so against the bar of four the pattern slides a beat each time round: a quiet phase shift built into the arithmetic. Sawtooth plucks in C minor keep it bright and percussive.

sounds.name: Four Against Five
sounds.ref: In the style of a gamelan’s interlocking metallophones
sounds.blurb: Bell tones in just C major: quarters against groups of five sixteenths, round every five beats.
sounds.how: Five against four takes twenty sixteenths to come back together, longer than a bar, so it never settles where you expect. Squares through a resonant filter ring like small gongs, and the just C major scale (8-JI) keeps every pair of notes pure.

sounds.name: Five Against Seven
sounds.ref: In the style of Conlon Nancarrow’s player-piano canons
sounds.blurb: Woody marimba notes, five against seven: a cycle of thirty-five sixteenths that no ear can count.
sounds.how: Nancarrow punched player-piano rolls with tempo ratios no pianist could play. Five against seven comes round only after thirty-five sixteenths, almost nine beats, so the two lines seem free of each other and of the bar, while the arithmetic keeps every note in place. Short, filtered squares sound like a marimba.

sounds.name: Accelerando
sounds.ref: In the style of Conlon Nancarrow’s tempo canons
sounds.blurb: A melody that speeds up through every bar over a steady beat: a slow wave patched into RHYTHM 1.
sounds.how: Nancarrow wrote player-piano canons whose voices run at tempos that speed up against each other. Here VCO 2, slowed into an LFO by Sequencer 2’s steady −5 V, sends its deepest sub’s rising sawtooth into RHYTHM 1: the divisor falls from ÷16 to ÷1 over about two seconds, so Sequencer 1’s notes accelerate from a bar apart to sixteenths, then snap back. Rhythm 4 keeps the beat on Sequencer 2, which is held, so it fires the envelopes without moving anything.

steps.title: VCO 2 as a slow wave
steps.why:

Patched into VCO 2’s input it drops VCO 2 five octaves, to about 8 Hz at the held C4 (a key transposes it, so another key moves the rate too), and its subs below a hertz. VCO 2 is not in the mix: it is a slow wave now, not a voice. Its SUB 2 at ÷16 rises once about every two seconds, a bar at this tempo.

- SEQ 2 STEP 1 -5 · -60 st
- SEQ 2 STEP 2 -5 · -60 st
- SEQ 2 STEP 3 -5 · -60 st
- SEQ 2 STEP 4 -5 · -60 st
- VCO 2 SUB 2 FREQ ÷16
- Patch SEQ 2 OUT to VCO 2 input
- Listen for: nothing new: VCO 2 is not heard.

sounds.name: Rhythmicon Ratios
sounds.ref: In the style of Henry Cowell’s Rhythmicon
sounds.blurb: Four rhythms in the ratios 2:3:4:5, each picking an undertone from its own sequencer.
sounds.how: Cowell and Theremin’s Rhythmicon (1931) played the overtone series as rhythm: a pitch twice as high pulsed twice as fast. Here all four rhythm generators run, ÷2 and ÷3 on Sequencer 1, ÷4 and ÷5 on Sequencer 2, and the sequencers move the subs’ divisors rather than the VCOs, so every hit lands on a different note of the undertone series. Rhythm and harmony come from the same whole numbers.

sounds.name: Hemiola Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Afro-Cuban bembé
sounds.blurb: A low bass on dotted quarters against a high answer on quarters: three against two in the bass.
sounds.how: A hemiola sets three beats against two. Rhythm 1 at ÷6 (dotted quarters) moves a bass built from VCO 1’s subs; Rhythm 2 at ÷4 (quarters) moves VCO 2 two octaves up. Every hit sounds both, so the bass is re-struck under the answers and the two meters argue in the low end.

sounds.name: Undertone Staircase

sounds.blurb: The subs climb the undertone series step by step, again and again: a slow wave in VCO 1 SUB.

sounds.name: Undertone Zap
sounds.ref: In the style of a chiptune arpeggio
sounds.blurb: Every note tumbles down the undertone series as it fades: the VCA EG patched into VCO 1 SUB.
sounds.how: An envelope at a SUB input lowers the divisors while it is high. Patch the VCA EG there with the subs at ÷16 and ÷13: each note starts at ÷4 and ÷1, as high as the envelope can push them, and steps down the undertones as it decays, a quick falling run inside every note. Sequencer 1 plays a two-against-three melody on VCO 1.

sounds.name: Undertone Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of a chapel organ’s foundation stops
sounds.blurb: A plain square-wave organ whose lower stops are VCO 1’s own subs, an octave and two octaves down.
sounds.how: An organ builds a full sound from pipes an octave apart. The Subharmonicon gets the same from one VCO: SUB 1 at ÷2 is the octave below and SUB 2 at ÷4 two octaves below, locked in phase so the three never beat. Square waves and a filter half open give the hollow, woody tone of flue pipes; a fast attack and a short decay make it speak and stop like an organ, holding while the key is down.

sounds.name: Mixtur Minor
sounds.ref: In the style of Oskar Sala’s Mixtur-Trautonium
sounds.blurb: Every note a minor chord: the fifth and sixth undertones under the note, as the Mixtur-Trautonium played them.
sounds.how: Divide a note by 4, 5 and 6 and you get a minor triad, the mirror of the major one the overtones make. Here VCO 1 sits at C5 with its subs at ÷5 and ÷6, so each key sounds the note high above a minor chord two octaves down. Oskar Sala built the Mixtur-Trautonium around exactly these divided tones; a soft filter swell on each note gives his slightly vocal colour.

VCO 2 a tiny fraction above VCO 1 makes the two saws drift against each other, the way his oscillators never quite held still; SUB 1 adds a quiet octave beneath. A resonant filter that the VCF EG pushes open on each note gives the vowel.

sounds.name: Audio-Rate PWM Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of a 1970s progressive-rock synth lead
sounds.blurb: A vocal, buzzing lead: silent VCO 1 a fifth up, patched into VCO 2’s PWM at audio rate.
sounds.how: A pulse width swept at audio rate adds sidebands, as FM does. VCO 1 OUT into VCO 2’s PWM, with VCO 1 a fifth above and silent: VCO 2’s width moves three times for every two of its cycles, giving a nasal, vowel-like tone that stays the same up and down the keys, since both VCOs follow them. Detune VCO 1 and the tone starts to move.

sounds.blurb: A bass that bites itself: VCA OUT patched back into CUTOFF.
sounds.how: Patch the synth’s own output into CUTOFF and the filter opens on every peak of the sound passing through it: feedback filter FM, a growl that follows the note and grows with the level. VOLUME now sets how hard it snarls as well as how loud it is.

sounds.name: Fifth-Root Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of a doom-metal bass tone
sounds.blurb: A heavy saw bass whose real root is the fifth below the note you play.
sounds.how: Divide C by 3 and you land on the F an octave and a fifth below. With SUB 2 at ÷3 loudest, the ear hears that F as the root and the key’s C as its fifth: the keyboard plays a fifth higher than it sounds. SUB 1 at ÷2 fills the octave between. Saws, a closed filter and a full mix drive the mixer into its warm overdrive.

sounds.name: Undertone Bloom
sounds.ref: In the style of Gérard Grisey’s spectral music
sounds.blurb: A pad whose upper chord climbs the undertone series as it swells: the VCA EG into VCO 2 SUB.
sounds.how: Grisey’s spectral music builds harmony from the series of a single note. Here VCO 2’s subs, centred deep at ÷12 and ÷16, are pushed up the undertone series by the VCA EG on a slow attack: as each note swells the chord above it climbs, step by just step, and as the note is let go it sinks back. VCO 1 holds the root steady underneath.

sounds.name: Filter-FM Piano

sounds.blurb: A bright, clanging electric piano: silent VCO 2 a ninth up, shaking the filter at audio rate.

sounds.name: Pulse Choir

sounds.name: Berlin Transposed
sounds.ref: In the style of Tangerine Dream’s Phaedra sequences
sounds.blurb: A pumping eighth-note bass sequence that the riff moves through C minor, A♭ and B♭, a bar at a time.
sounds.how: Tangerine Dream set a Moog sequencer running and changed key by playing one note on the keyboard. Here Sequencer 1 plays a four-note bass figure on eighths, VCO 1’s subs underneath; the riff holds a C for two bars, then A♭, then B♭, and every held key transposes the running figure without restarting it. Pick a library bass line in the sequencer and it transposes the figure the same way.

sounds.name: Poly Rock
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s Poly Rock patch
sounds.blurb: Sub chords stepped by both sequencers, with a drum pulse from CLOCK OUT.
sounds.how: The manual’s Poly Rock tunes the four subs to chord shapes and patches CLOCK OUT into the VCA input for “drums”: every clock opens the amplifier a little on its own, a beat under the sequenced chords. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Cloud Path
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s Cloud Path patch
sounds.blurb: Slow, soft chords from both sequencers, with no cables at all.
sounds.how: The manual’s Cloud Path uses no cables: both sequencers and all four subs, tuned with their levels open, then faded in while it plays; RHYTHM 3 SEQ 1 doubles Sequencer 1’s pace. Long envelopes blur each step into the next. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Aquatic Chords
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s Aquatic Chords patch
sounds.blurb: Each sequencer plays the other VCO, and the envelopes bend the rhythms.
sounds.how: The manual’s Aquatic Chords crosses the sequencers over, SEQ 1 into VCO 2 and SEQ 2 into VCO 1, patches the two envelopes into Rhythms 1 and 2 so each note changes the next rhythm, and fires the envelopes from SEQ 1 CLK alone. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Point Zero
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s Point Zero patch
sounds.blurb: Each sequencer rewrites its own rhythm, with the clocks playing filter and VCA.
sounds.how: The manual’s Point Zero feeds each sequencer back into a rhythm generator (SEQ 1 into RHYTHM 1, SEQ 2 into RHYTHM 2), so every step changes when the next one comes, and patches SEQ 1 CLK into CUTOFF and SEQ 2 CLK into the VCA. VCF ATTACK sets how long each sweep takes. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Three Hands on the Wheel

Its sequencer pitches are suggestions. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Bateria
sounds.ref: In the style of the manual’s Bateria patch
sounds.blurb: A pitched kick from the filter and envelopes, its tuning set by Sequencer 1.
sounds.how: The manual’s Bateria (Portuguese for a drum kit) turns the synth into a kick: SEQ 1 into CUTOFF tunes each hit, SEQ 2 into VCO 1 PWM changes its texture, and VCF DECAY and EG AMT give it its flavour. Short envelopes and a resonant filter swept down do the drumming. The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.

sounds.name: Spiral Ways

sounds.name: Star-Gate

sounds.blurb: High, glittering sequences whose third rhythm the filter envelope keeps moving.

The manual’s patch sheet transcribes the cables; its knobs and buttons are drawn, not written, so the settings here are this lesson’s.
